claim: Working memory is a critical brain function for maintaining and manipulating information over delay periods of seconds.
source: Working memory is a critical brain function for maintaining and manipulating information over delay periods of seconds.
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by established scientific knowledge about working memory.

claim: It is debated whether delay-period neural activity in sensory regions is important for the active maintenance of information during the delay period.
source: It is debated whether delay-period neural activity in sensory regions is important for the active maintenance of information during the delay period.
evidence: This statement references an ongoing scientific debate, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Optogenetic suppression of neuronal activity in APC during the delay period impaired performance in all the tasks.
source: Optogenetic suppression of neuronal activity in APC during the delay period impaired performance in all the tasks.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1-4.

claim: APC neuronal populations encoded odor information in the delay period even with an intervening distracting task.
source: Furthermore, electrophysiological recordings revealed that APC neuronal populations encoded odor information in the delay period even with an intervening distracting task.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by electrophysiological recording data presented in Figures 5-7.

claim: Delay activity in APC is important for active information maintenance in olfactory working memory.
source: Thus, delay activity in APC is important for active information maintenance in olfactory working memory.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by both optogenetic and electrophysiological data.

claim: Originally the prefrontal cortex was thought to be the specific site for WM.
source: Originally the prefrontal cortex was thought to be the specific site for WM (Jacobsen, 1935).
evidence: This is a historical statement supported by citation to Jacobsen, 1935.

claim: Later results suggested that parallel distributed circuits are responsible for WM.
source: However, later results suggested that parallel distributed circuits are responsible for WM (D'Esposito and Postle, 2015; Eriksson et al., 2015; Christophel et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to recent literature.

claim: The delay-period activity of the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) of mice is only important during the learning but not the well-trained phase in an olfactory WM task.
source: Previously, we have shown that the delay-period activity of the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) of mice is only important during the learning but not the well-trained phase in an olfactory WM task (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from previous work by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: The 'essential theory' stressed the importance of sensory cortices in WM.
source: On the one hand, the 'essential theory' stressed the importance of sensory cortices in WM (Pasternak and Greenlee, 2005; Scimeca et al., 2018; Gayet et al., 2018), arguing that it is more parsimonious to receive, process, and maintain information in the same regions.
evidence: This describes one side of a theoretical debate, supported by citations.

claim: Some recording and functional imaging experiments supported the hypothesis that sensory cortices can exhibit information-selective delay-period activity in WM tasks.
source: Some recording and functional imaging experiments supported the hypothesis that sensory cortices can exhibit information-selective delay-period activity in WM tasks (Pasternak and Greenlee, 2005; Fuster and Jervey, 1981; Miyashita and Chang, 1988; Harrison and Tong, 2009; Mendoza-Halliday et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement summarizes findings from multiple cited studies.

claim: Perturbation of neural activity in sensory areas can impair WM performance.
source: Furthermore, perturbation of neural activity in sensory areas can impair WM performance (Pasternak and Greenlee, 2005; Colombo et al., 1990; Harris et al., 2002; Seidemann et al., 1998; Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement summarizes findings from multiple cited studies.

claim: The 'unessential theory' stressed that sustained activity emerges as a property of association cortices, but is not present in early sensory cortices, at least in the visual, somatosensory, and auditory domains.
source: On the other hand, the 'unessential theory' stressed that sustained activity emerges as a property of association cortices, but is not present in early sensory cortices, at least in the visual, somatosensory, and auditory domains (Mendoza-Halliday et al., 2014; van Kerkoerle et al., 2017; Leavitt et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the opposing theoretical position, supported by citations.

claim: A distractor presented during the delay period diminished delay-period sustained activity in sensory cortices without changing performance.
source: More importantly, a distractor presented during the delay period diminished delay-period sustained activity in sensory cortices without changing performance (Miller et al., 1996; Bettencourt and Xu, 2016), arguing that sensory cortices may not be important for WM tasks (Xu, 2018).
evidence: This statement summarizes findings from cited studies that support the 'unessential theory'.

claim: A hallmark of WM is a progressive decay of performance with increasing delay duration.
source: A hallmark of WM is a progressive decay of performance with increasing delay duration (Baddeley, 2012), which was indeed observed in the task (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is a known characteristic of working memory supported by citation and confirmed by data in Figure 1d.

claim: Mice readily performed the DNMS task with little licking during the delay period.
source: Mice readily performed the task with little licking during the delay period (Figure 1c, Video 1, Video 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the behavioral experiments, supported by figure and video references.

claim: The majority of the APC neurons (79%, 82 out of 104) were suppressed during the optogenetic stimulation.
source: The majority of the APC neurons (79%, 82 out of 104) were suppressed during the optogenetic stimulation, while a small fraction (12%, 12 out of 104) were activated; the optogenetic effect diminished within 1 s after laser-offset (see the third dotted line marked 1 s after laser-offset in Figure 1f; spike-sorting quality in Figure 1—figure supplement 3; and example single neurons showing activity modulation induced by optogenetic perturbation in Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from op-tetrode recordings, supported by data in figures.

claim: Performance was impaired following optogenetic suppression of the APC delay-period activity in the VGAT-ChR2 mice, with delay duration of 5, 8, or 12 s.
source: Performance was impaired following optogenetic suppression of the APC delay-period activity in the VGAT-ChR2 mice, with delay duration of 5, 8, or 12 s (Figure 1h–j; for effect size and complete ANOVA statistics, see Figure 1—figure supplement 5i–m and Figure 1—source data 1, 2).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in multiple figures.

claim: Optogenetic suppression in trials with longer delay duration resulted in larger deficits.
source: Moreover, optogenetic suppression in trials with longer delay duration resulted in larger deficits (Figure 1h–j).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Behavioral deficits were reflected as an increased false-alarm rate and a decreased discriminability (d').
source: Behavioral deficits were reflected as an increased false-alarm rate and a decreased discriminability (d') (false alarm rate for all delay durations, d' for 8 s and 12 s delay durations, Figure 1l,n, Figure 1—figure supplement 5, b,f and h, Figure 1—source data 1, 2).
evidence: This describes specific behavioral metrics affected by optogenetic manipulation, supported by data in figures.

claim: The lick efficiency was impaired in laser-on trials in the VGAT-ChR2 mice.
source: Similarly, the lick efficiency (the percentage of successful licks with reward) was impaired in laser-on trials in the VGAT-ChR2 mice (Figure 1m, Figure 1—figure supplement 5, c and g, Figure 1—source data 1, 2).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding supported by data in the referenced figures.

claim: Optogenetic suppression of APC neuronal activity was varied in both duration (3, 6, 10, or 12 s) and temporal position (early, mid or late in the delay period) in a trial-by-trial fashion.
source: Specifically, optogenetic suppression of APC neuronal activity was varied in both duration (3, 6, 10, or 12 s) and temporal position (early, mid or late in the delay period) in a trial-by-trial fashion.
evidence: This describes the experimental design for testing the effects of optogenetic manipulation timing.

claim: Optogenetic suppression significantly impaired the DNMS task performance in VGAT-ChR2 mice, especially for laser illumination during the late-delay period.
source: Optogenetic suppression significantly impaired the DNMS task performance in VGAT-ChR2 mice, especially for laser illumination during the late-delay period (Figure 2b,d, Figure 2—source data 1,2).
evidence: This is a finding from the varied optogenetic stimulation experiments, supported by data in figures.

claim: In the laser-on trials for VGAT-ChR2 mice, the duration and timing of laser illumination had a significant interaction in determining the task correct rates, false alarm rates and miss rates.
source: Furthermore, in the laser-on trials for VGAT-ChR2 mice, the duration and timing of laser illumination had a significant interaction in determining the task correct rates, false alarm rates and miss rates (Figure 2b–e, Figure 2—source data 1,2).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis of optogenetic manipulation effects.

claim: Optogenetic suppression of longer laser-on duration during a later phase of the delay period results in larger behavioral defects.
source: Therefore, optogenetic suppression of longer laser-on duration during a later phase of the delay period results in larger behavioral defects.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on timing and duration of optogenetic manipulation.

claim: We observed significant effect of delay duration on DNMS task performance, independent of genotype.
source: We observed significant effect of delay duration on DNMS task performance, independent of genotype (Figure 2g, Figure 2—figure supplement 1c and d, Figure 2—source data 2,3).
evidence: This is a finding from the varied delay duration experiments, supported by data in figures.

claim: Optogenetic suppression impaired task performance only in VGAT-ChR2 mice.
source: Consistent with previous results, optogenetic suppression impaired task performance only in VGAT-ChR2 mice (Figure 2g, Figure 2—figure supplement 1c and d, Figure 2—source data 2,3).
evidence: This confirms the specificity of the optogenetic effect to the experimental group.

claim: We did not observe significant interaction between delay-period duration and laser on/off.
source: We did not observe significant interaction between delay-period duration and laser on/off (Figure 2g, Figure 2—figure supplement 1c and d, Figure 2—source data 2,3).
evidence: This is a negative finding from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Longer delay duration does not result in different behavioral impairment induced by optogenetic suppression of fixed duration.
source: Therefore, longer delay duration does not result in different behavioral impairment induced by optogenetic suppression of fixed duration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lack of interaction between delay duration and optogenetic effect.

claim: We observed intact behavioral performance when APC activity was suppressed before odor delivery in three control tasks.
source: In all three tasks, we observed intact behavioral performance (Figure 3a–f, Figure 3—source data 1–2; effect size, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is a finding from control experiments designed to test whether optogenetic effects are specific to delay-period maintenance.

claim: The lack of behavioral impairment in all three control experiments excluded the perception-impairment hypothesis.
source: The lack of behavioral impairment in all three control experiments excluded the perception-impairment hypothesis (Figure 3—source data 1–2).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the control experiments.

claim: The behavioral deficits following optogenetic perturbation of APC delay-period activity reflected the contribution of this activity to information maintenance in the DNMS task.
source: Therefore, the behavioral deficits following optogenetic perturbation of APC delay-period activity reflected the contribution of this activity to information maintenance in the DNMS task.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combination of main experiments and control experiments.

claim: The optimal model (#6) contained only four key parameters and the interactions among them: optogenetic suppression or not during the delay period, match or non-match relationship, and the delay duration (coupled with laser-on duration).
source: By eliminating less-predictive variables, we obtained the optimal model (#6, AIC value significantly smaller than all other models; Figure 3g–i, Figure 3—source data 3 and 4), which contained only four key parameters and the interactions among them: optogenetic suppression or not during the delay period, match or non-match relationship, and the delay duration (coupled with laser-on duration).
evidence: This describes the results of formal model comparison analysis.

claim: The association between the WM delay perturbation and the delay duration is consistent with the important role of APC delay activity in information maintenance.
source: This association between the WM delay perturbation and the delay duration is consistent with the important role of APC delay activity in information maintenance (Figure 3j).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model comparison results.

claim: The impact of optogenetic perturbation out-weighted that of delay duration.
source: Quantitatively, the impact of optogenetic perturbation out-weighted that of delay duration (Figure 3j).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the model comparison analysis.

claim: The DNMS task in monkeys can be performed through a recency effect and with little selective memory maintenance.
source: For example, it has also been suggested that the DNMS task in monkeys can be performed through a recency effect and with little selective memory maintenance (Wittig and Richmond, 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study that raises concerns about the DNMS task.

claim: The activity of a sensory cortex can be suppressed or enhanced following the repetition of a sensory stimulus.
source: Furthermore, the activity of a sensory cortex can be suppressed or enhanced following the repetition of a sensory stimulus (Miller et al., 1993).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study about sensory adaptation.

claim: Successful performance of the DPA task required WM maintenance and learning of the arbitrary association between the odor pairs.
source: Successful performance of the task required WM maintenance and learning of the arbitrary association between the odor pairs.
evidence: This describes the cognitive demands of the DPA task.

claim: Repetition or recency effects cannot be used to solve the DPA task, because the sample odor is not repeated within a trial.
source: Importantly, repetition (Miller et al., 1993) or recency effects (Wittig and Richmond, 2014) cannot be used to solve the task, because the sample odor is not repeated within a trial.
evidence: This is a logical argument about the design of the DPA task.

claim: Mice readily learned the DPA task.
source: Mice readily learned the task (Figure 4d, black curve).
evidence: This is an observation from the behavioral experiments, supported by figure reference.

claim: Optogenetic suppression of APC delay-period activity impaired DPA performance.
source: Critically, optogenetic suppression of APC delay-period activity impaired DPA performance (Figure 4b, Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–d, Figure 4—source data 1,2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the DPA task experiments, supported by data in figures.

claim: We did not find outliers in optogenetic impairment in DPA performance with two widely used statistical methods.
source: Although optogenetic impairment in DPA performance (difference in correct rate between laser-on and laser-off trials) varied across mice, we did not find outliers with two widely used statistical methods: (1) for elements more than 1.5 interquartile ranges above the upper quartile or below the lower quartile (Hattori et al., 2017; Kato et al., 2013; Sreenivasan et al., 2016); and (2) Grubb's method (Namburi et al., 2015; Burgos-Robles et al., 2017; Carus-Cadavieco et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes statistical analysis performed to validate the data quality.

claim: The APC delay-period activity is important for WM maintenance, even in a task without repeating sensory cues.
source: Therefore, the APC delay-period activity is important for WM maintenance, even in a task without repeating sensory cues.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DPA task results.

claim: A hallmark of active maintenance in WM is resistance against distractors during the delay period.
source: A hallmark of active maintenance in WM is resistance against distractors during the delay period (Baddeley, 2012; Miller et al., 1996; Bettencourt and Xu, 2016).
evidence: This is a known characteristic of working memory supported by citations.

claim: The dual-task paradigm belongs to the dual-task designs that have been used to study central executive control.
source: This paradigm belongs to the dual-task designs that have been used to study central executive control (Baddeley, 2012; Watanabe and Funahashi, 2018; Watanabe and Funahashi, 2014), because mice are required to split attention in the middle of the delay period in order to perform the GNG task, while simultaneously maintaining the sample information of the DPA task (Figure 4c).
evidence: This describes the theoretical framework for the dual-task design, supported by citations.

claim: DPA performance in the dual-task paradigm was worse than that in the simple DPA task even in the well-trained phase.
source: DPA performance in the dual-task paradigm was worse than that in the simple DPA task even in the well-trained phase (Figure 4d,f), consistent with the dual-task interference observed in humans (Baddeley, 2012) and monkeys (Watanabe and Funahashi, 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from the dual-task experiments, supported by data in figures and consistent with cited literature.

claim: Interference was dependent on the trial types inserted in the DPA delay, with the worst performance for the Go-distractor trials.
source: Moreover, interference was dependent on the trial types inserted in the DPA delay, with the worst performance for the Go-distractor trials (Figure 4f).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of different distractor conditions in the dual-task.

claim: The DPA false-alarm rate within the dual task increased significantly in the laser-on trials in the VGAT-ChR2 group.
source: The DPA false-alarm rate within the dual task increased significantly in the laser-on trials in the VGAT-ChR2 group (Figure 4h).
evidence: This is a finding from optogenetic manipulation during the dual-task, supported by data in figure.

claim: APC delay-period activity is important for active maintenance in the face of distraction from an intervening task.
source: Therefore, APC delay-period activity is important for active maintenance in the face of distraction from an intervening task.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dual-task optogenetic experiments.

claim: A subset of APC neurons showed selective activity following exposure to different sample odors during the delay period in correct trials.
source: A subset of APC neurons showed selective activity following exposure to different sample odors during the delay period in correct trials (for examples, see Figure 5a–c, Figure 5—figure supplement 2a–i).
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiological recordings, supported by data in figures.

claim: Some APC neurons were able to code for the sample information in single trials.
source: Some of these neurons were able to code for the sample information in single trials (Figure 5c and d, Figure 5—figure supplement 2c,f and i, as measured by the area under receiver operating characteristic, auROC).
evidence: This is a finding from single-neuron analysis, supported by data in figures.

claim: In error trials, the coding ability of these neurons was reduced.
source: In error trials, the coding ability of these neurons was reduced (as measured by auROC, Figure 5c and d, Figure 5—figure supplement 2b-i).
evidence: This is a finding showing correlation between neural activity and behavioral performance.

claim: APC neuronal activity encodes WM information and is correlated with task performance.
source: Thus, APC neuronal activity encodes WM information and is correlated with task performance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electrophysiological recording data.

claim: More than 25% (in 4-s delay trials) and 40% (in 8-s delay trials) of single units in the APC showed sample-odor selectivity in firing rate at the beginning of the delay period.
source: More than 25% (in 4-s delay trials) and 40% (in 8-s delay trials) of single units in the APC showed sample-odor selectivity in firing rate at the beginning of the delay period, and about 10% of single units were selective at the end of the delay period (Figure 5g–i and Figure 5—figure supplement 3c–e).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from analysis of single-unit recordings.

claim: About 10% of single units were selective at the end of the delay period.
source: More than 25% (in 4-s delay trials) and 40% (in 8-s delay trials) of single units in the APC showed sample-odor selectivity in firing rate at the beginning of the delay period, and about 10% of single units were selective at the end of the delay period (Figure 5g–i and Figure 5—figure supplement 3c–e).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from analysis of single-unit recordings.

claim: A population decoding analysis based on support vector machines demonstrated significant single-trial decoding of sample-odor identity in APC delay activity.
source: A population decoding analysis (bootstrap leave-one-trial-out cross-validation accuracy) based on support vector machines (SVM) also demonstrated significant single-trial decoding of sample-odor identity in APC delay activity (Figure 5j and k).
evidence: This is a finding from population-level decoding analysis, supported by data in figures.

claim: The fraction of sample selective neuron in the APC was greater in the 8s-delay task than in the 4s-delay task.
source: It is nonetheless interesting to see that the fraction of sample selective neuron in the APC was greater in the 8s-delay task than in the 4s-delay task (Figure 5—figure supplement 3f), both in the total fraction of selective neurons (sample-selective for more than 0.5 s) and in the subpopulation that showed longer persistent selectivity (sample-selective for more than 5 s).
evidence: This is a comparative finding between different delay durations, supported by data in figure.

claim: The dynamics of the decoding accuracy in the 8s-delay-tasks was not a passive continuation of the decoding accuracy in the 4 s task.
source: Furthermore, the dynamics of the decoding accuracy in the 8s-delay-tasks was not a passive continuation of the decoding accuracy in the 4 s task, as the decoding accuracy at 5 s since sample onset was much higher in the 8 s task (~85%, Figure 5k) than in the 4 s task (~70%, Figure 5j), consistent with the active recruitment of neurons for the maintenance of information in accordance with task requirements.
evidence: This is a finding from comparison of decoding dynamics across different delay durations.

claim: Significant decoding was observed in the off-diagonal space in tasks with both 4-s and 8 s delay periods, suggesting stable maintenance of WM information by APC neuronal activity throughout the delay period.
source: In the CTD analysis of APC neuronal activity, significant decoding was observed in the off-diagonal space in tasks with both 4-s and 8 s delay periods, suggesting stable maintenance of WM information by APC neuronal activity throughout the delay period.
evidence: This is a finding from cross-temporal decoding analysis.

claim: The number of stimuli used for training can bias the strategies of the animals.
source: It has been shown that the number of stimuli used for training can bias the strategies of the animals (Slotnick, 2001), and this limits the generality of the results when using just two odorants as the sample odors.
evidence: This is a consideration from cited literature that motivated the multiple-sample DPA task.

claim: Despite an initial relearning each day, mice performed the multiple-sample DPA task well.
source: Despite an initial relearning each day, mice performed this task well (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is an observation from the behavioral experiments, supported by figure reference.

claim: Many neurons showed sample-odor information during the delay period in the multiple-sample DPA task, as revealed by mutual information.
source: As for the DNMS task with two sample odors, we observed many neurons with sample-odor information during the delay period, as revealed by mutual information (MI, Figure 6c, see Materials and methods), which measures the degree to which responses are informative about the identity of the stimulus.
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiological recordings in the multiple-sample DPA task.

claim: Even after the distracting task during the delay period, APC population activity still coded the DPA samples and GNG distractors.
source: Even after the distracting task during the delay period, APC population activity still coded the DPA samples and GNG distractors, as shown in the MI analysis of one example neuron in Figure 7a.
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiological recordings during the dual-task.

claim: Approximately 30% of neurons can code for both the DPA samples and the GNG odors in the APC neuronal population.
source: In the APC neuronal population, approximately 30% of neurons can code for both the DPA samples and the GNG odors (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from analysis of dual-task recordings.

claim: One can decode the DPA sample odors in the dual-task design in the trials without distractor, with the No-go distractor, or with the Go distractor.
source: In the SVM decoding analysis based on APC neuronal activity during the later delay period after the distracting task, one can decode the DPA sample odors in the dual-task design in the trials without distractor, with the No-go distractor, or with the Go distractor (Figure 7c–e).
evidence: This is a finding from decoding analysis of dual-task recordings.

claim: The SVM decoding accuracy during the delay period after the distractor task was related to the distractor type and to performance in the distractor task.
source: Interestingly, we observed that the SVM decoding accuracy during the delay period after the distractor task was also related to the distractor type and to performance in the distractor task (Figure 7f), suggesting that APC selectivity is important for performance in the DPA task in the dual-task design.
evidence: This is a finding showing correlation between neural decoding and behavioral performance in the dual-task.

claim: The APC is a good candidate for olfactory WM because it is directly connected with the olfactory bulb.
source: The APC is a good candidate because it is directly connected with the olfactory bulb (Ghosh et al., 2011; Miyamichi et al., 2011; Sosulski et al., 2011; Bekkers and Suzuki, 2013; Price and Powell, 1970; Davison and Ehlers, 2011), encodes odor information (Bekkers and Suzuki, 2013; Schoenbaum and Eichenbaum, 1995; Wilson, 1998; Poo and Isaacson, 2009; Stettler and Axel, 2009; Shusterman et al., 2011; Miura et al., 2012; Courtiol and Wilson, 2017; Zhan and Luo, 2010; Gire et al., 2013; Iurilli and Datta, 2017; Bolding and Franks, 2017; Otazu et al., 2015), and is important for olfactory behavior (Bekkers and Suzuki, 2013; Miura et al., 2012; Courtiol and Wilson, 2017; Choi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a rationale for studying APC, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The rich recurrent connectivity within the APC is well suited for generating reverberating activity that outlasts sensory inputs.
source: The rich recurrent connectivity within the APC (Bekkers and Suzuki, 2013; Franks et al., 2011; Bolding and Franks, 2018) is also well suited for generating reverberating activity that outlasts sensory inputs (Major and Tank, 2004).
evidence: This is a theoretical consideration supported by citations about APC anatomy and physiology.

claim: Activity patterns of the APC neurons are critically dependent on olfactory experience, indicating an active involvement.
source: In addition, activity patterns of the APC neurons are critically dependent on olfactory experience, indicating an active involvement (Wilson, 1998; Courtiol and Wilson, 2017; Saar et al., 1999; Roesch et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a characteristic of APC supported by citations.

claim: The piriform cortex is activated in a human olfactory WM task.
source: Finally, the piriform cortex is also activated in a human olfactory WM task (Zelano et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited human neuroimaging study.

claim: Only about 10% of APC neurons carried WM information during the late delay period.
source: We observed that only about 10% of APC neurons carried WM information during the late delay period (Figure 5g and i).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The small percentage of APC neurons that are involved in coding the maintained information is consistent with the sparse coding previously observed in piriform cortex.
source: The small percentage of APC neurons that are involved in coding the maintained information is consistent with the sparse coding previously observed in piriform cortex (Poo and Isaacson, 2009; Stettler and Axel, 2009; Miura et al., 2012) (but see Bolding and Franks, 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of previous literature.

claim: Although the APC activity is constantly updated by ongoing sensory inputs, this sensory cortex could resist overwriting and could maintain information through population activity in the WM tasks, even when a distracting task is performed during the delay period.
source: Therefore, although the APC activity is constantly updated by ongoing sensory inputs, this sensory cortex could resist overwriting and could maintain information through population activity in the WM tasks, even when a distracting task is performed during the delay period.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dual-task recording results.

claim: Our experimental data are consistent with the prediction that temporal suppression of the delay-period activity of an early sensory region should produce behavioral defects if sensory regions are essential for WM maintenance.
source: Our experimental data are consistent with this latter prediction, suggesting that a sensory region can be important for olfactory WM.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in the context of the theoretical debate.

claim: Our optogenetic suppression was quite focal and spared large areas of APC, as shown by the reduction in c-Fos stained active neurons.
source: One possibility may be that our optogenetic suppression was quite focal and spared large areas of APC, as shown by the reduction in c-Fos stained active neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This is an observation from immunohistochemistry data.

claim: The simpler tasks with shorter-delay duration imposed less demand on APC delay-period activity, and the remaining unaffected areas within APC might be sufficient to maintain the information.
source: Therefore the simpler tasks with shorter-delay duration imposed less demand on APC delay-period activity, and the remaining unaffected areas within APC might be sufficient to maintain the information.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the smaller effect sizes with shorter delays.

claim: There could be a loop of activity involving APC and other regions.
source: Another possibility is that there could be a loop of activity involving APC and other regions (see below for more discussion).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed effects.

claim: The partial optogenetic suppression could act like a damper on recurrent activity, with a slow decay rate.
source: Moreover, the partial optogenetic suppression could act like a damper on recurrent activity, with a slow decay rate.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation for the observed effects.

claim: Bolkan et al. (2017) showed that optogenetic silencing of the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) impaired spatial WM performance in a task with 60 s but not 10 s delay duration.
source: For example, Bolkan et al. (2017) showed that optogenetic silencing of the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) impaired spatial WM performance in a task with 60 s but not 10 s delay duration.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study that is consistent with the current results.

claim: The designs of the DNMS and DPA tasks are quite different, for example, the DPA task requires the association between sample and test odors, which is not required for the DNMS task.
source: The designs of the two tasks are quite different, for example, the DPA task requires the association between sample and test odors, which is not required for the DNMS task.
evidence: This is a description of task differences.

claim: The neural circuit for the DPA task might be different from that for the DNMS task.
source: Therefore, the neural circuit for the DPA task might be different from that for the DNMS task, which remains to be determined in future studies.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential circuit differences.

claim: The olfactory pathway downstream from the olfactory bulb is organized in a highly parallel manner.
source: The olfactory pathway downstream from the olfactory bulb is organized in a highly parallel manner, as mitral/tufted neurons in the olfactory bulb project to multiple brain regions, including the APC, the anterior olfactory nucleus, the cortical amygdala, the olfactory tubercle, and the lateral entorhinal cortex (Ghosh et al., 2011; Miyamichi et al., 2011; Sosulski et al., 2011; Price and Powell, 1970; Davison and Ehlers, 2011).
evidence: This is anatomical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: It was surprising that optogenetic perturbation of just one out of five parallel olfactory brain regions can impair olfactory WM performance.
source: Therefore, it was surprising that optogenetic perturbation of just one out of these five brain regions can impair olfactory WM performance, suggesting the importance for WM of the APC among the parallel olfactory pathways.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in the context of olfactory pathway anatomy.

claim: Other brain regions may contribute to the maintenance of sensory information in a WM task.
source: Other brain regions may contribute to the maintenance of sensory information in a WM task (as discussed in the previous section).
evidence: This acknowledges the possibility of distributed circuits.

claim: The hypothetical existence of other regions contributing to WM does not conflict with the current results showing that a sensory region plays important roles in WM maintenance.
source: The hypothetical existence of these regions does not conflict with the current results showing that a sensory region plays important roles in WM maintenance.
evidence: This is a logical argument about the interpretation of the results.

claim: The exact mechanism underlying the distributed neural circuit that underlies WM remains to be determined in the future.
source: The exact mechanism underlying the distributed neural circuit that underlies WM remains to be determined in the future.
evidence: This acknowledges limitations and future directions.

claim: The functional role of other sensory regions and the potential interaction between the APC and the mPFC in the learning and well-trained phases of WM tasks remain to be determined.
source: Furthermore, the functional role of other sensory regions (Ghosh et al., 2011; Miyamichi et al., 2011; Sosulski et al., 2011; Price and Powell, 1970; Davison and Ehlers, 2011) and the potential interaction between the APC and the mPFC (Liu et al., 2014) in the learning and well-trained phases of WM tasks remain to be determined.
evidence: This acknowledges limitations and future directions.

claim: The functional role of memory maintenance may be partially transferred from the mPFC to the APC through learning.
source: Thus, the functional role of memory maintenance may be partially transferred from the mPFC to the APC through learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing current results with previous findings.

claim: The underlying mechanisms of the transfer and the potential involvement of other brain regions remain to be determined.
source: The underlying mechanisms of the transfer and the potential involvement of other brain regions remain to be determined.
evidence: This acknowledges limitations and future directions.

claim: The dual-task design explicitly challenges the central executive control ability of a subject.
source: The dual-task design (Figure 4c) explicitly challenges the central executive control ability of a subject (reviewed by Baddeley, 2012; Watanabe and Funahashi, 2018).
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the dual-task design, supported by citations.

claim: The dual-task design is an important tool to study the distributed nature of WM maintenance, which could depend on task complexity.
source: It is an important tool to study the distributed nature of WM maintenance, which could depend on task complexity (Christophel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a theoretical statement supported by citation.

claim: A simpler sensory memory task could be more dependent on a sensory cortex than a more complex task.
source: A simpler sensory memory task could be more dependent on a sensory cortex than a more complex task.
evidence: This is a theoretical consideration about task complexity.

claim: If suppressing the delay activity of a sensory cortex in the dual task could impair WM performance, it will certainly implicate this sensory region in active information maintenance in WM.
source: Thus, if suppressing the delay activity of a sensory cortex in the dual task could impair WM performance, it will certainly implicate this sensory region in active information maintenance in WM.
evidence: This is a logical argument about the interpretation of dual-task results.

claim: Most of the previous dual-task studies have focused on prefrontal cortex.
source: Most of the previous studies have focused on prefrontal cortex (Watanabe and Funahashi, 2014; D'Esposito et al., 1995; Baddeley et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a statement about the literature, supported by citations.

claim: The delay-period activity of a sensory cortex can maintain sample information after the distracting task.
source: Here, we show that the delay-period activity of a sensory cortex can maintain sample information after the distracting task, and that suppressing this activity resulted in performance impairments (e.g. significantly increased false-alarm rate).
evidence: This is a summary of the dual-task findings.

claim: The delay-period activity of this sensory cortex is involved in dual-task performance.
source: Therefore the delay-period activity of this sensory cortex is involved in dual-task performance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dual-task results.

claim: Neuronal activity in the APC is associated with olfactory perception, but it also varies depending on brain states, task design, or learning experience.
source: Neuronal activity in the APC is associated with olfactory perception, but it also varies depending on brain states, task design, or learning experience (Courtiol and Wilson, 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about APC properties supported by citation.

claim: The APC has long been suggested to be an associative sensory region.
source: For this reason, the APC has long been suggested to be an associative sensory region (Bekkers and Suzuki, 2013; Courtiol and Wilson, 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about APC function supported by citations.

claim: The results demonstrated the importance of the APC activity beyond sensory perception.
source: Consistent with this notion, our results demonstrated the importance of the APC activity beyond sensory perception.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings.

claim: The results underscore the importance of the olfactory sensory cortex in memory maintenance beyond immediate sensory processing.
source: In summary, our results underscore the importance of the olfactory sensory cortex in memory maintenance beyond immediate sensory processing.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: VGAT-ChR2 mice have been used extensively in many studies to suppress local excitatory neurons.
source: The VGAT-ChR2 mice have been used extensively in many studies to suppress local excitatory neurons (e.g. Liu et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the methodology supported by citations.

claim: The first odor residue was briskly cleared at the beginning of the delay period.
source: The first odor residue was briskly cleared (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, the delay-period residual concentration is lower than the sensory threshold for this task [Liu et al., 2014]) at the beginning of the delay period.
evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by data in supplementary figure and citation.

claim: The delay-period residual concentration is lower than the sensory threshold for the DNMS task.
source: The first odor residue was briskly cleared (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, the delay-period residual concentration is lower than the sensory threshold for this task [Liu et al., 2014]) at the beginning of the delay period.
evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by data in supplementary figure and citation.

claim: Licking following the non-match trials led to water reward in the DNMS task.
source: Licking following the non-match trials (S1-S2, or S2-S1) led to water reward.
evidence: This describes the reward contingency in the DNMS task.

claim: No explicit punishment was applied for the error trials in the DNMS task.
source: No explicit punishment was applied for the error trials.
evidence: This describes the task design.

claim: The performance of control mice could be affected by light illumination with longer duration, probably through distraction by visual illumination.
source: Note that the performance of control mice could also be affected by light illumination with longer duration, for example 10 s laser-on condition in the DNMS task with 12 s delay, probably through distraction by visual illumination.
evidence: This is an observation and interpretation of a control effect.

claim: A visual mask was applied to diminish the visual distraction induced by laser illumination.
source: A visual mask was applied to diminish the visual distraction induced by laser illumination (as seen in Figure 1j).
evidence: This describes a methodological control.
